---
title: "Chloropleth Maps"
format: html
---


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)
library(mdsr)
library(maps)
library(viridis)
library(leaflet)
library(sf) 
library(rvest)
library(polite)
library(htmltools)
library(glue)
library(ggthemes)

library(maps)
states_polygon <- as_tibble(map_data("state")) |>
  select(region, group, order, lat, long)

# This will serve as the basis for our static map

states_sf <- 
  read_sf("https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/json/us-states.geojson") |>
  select(name, geometry)

# This will serve as the basis for our interactive geometry map


library(poliscidata)   
polisci_data <- as_tibble(poliscidata::states)


us_states <- map_data("state")

```






```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

alcohol_states <- 
  (as_tibble(poliscidata::states)) |>
  select(state, alcohol) |>
  mutate(
    state = str_to_lower(
      str_squish(state)
      )) 
# To look at states with alcohol statistics, we select only the alcohol variable with the state name. We then convert the state names to only lowercase, without spaces


states_polygon <- 
  states_polygon |>
  mutate(
    state = str_remove_all(
      region, 
      " ")
    ) |>
  select(-region)
# We form our static state information by renaming the region variable to state, and converting all state names to lowercase without spaces


states_sf <- 
  states_sf |>
  mutate(
    state = str_to_lower(
      name)
    ) |>
  mutate(
    state = str_remove_all(
      state, 
      " ")
    ) |>
  select(-name)
# We perform the same process on the interactive geometry set, so that it may be joined with the polysci data
```


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

alc_static <- 
  left_join(
    states_polygon, 
    alcohol_states, 
    by = "state")
# We simply join the static state information with the alcohol stats by the state column.


alc_int <- 
  left_join(
    states_sf, 
    alcohol_states, 
    by = "state") |>
  mutate(
    label = str_c(
      "The alcohol consumption of ", 
      state, 
      " is ", 
      alcohol, 
      " gal/capita")
    ) |>
  filter(!is.na(alcohol))
# We do the same for our interactive plot, however, we create a new label column that describes the statistic for each state, so that we can have a hovering label for our interactive plot. We also remove any states regions that don't have a matching alcohol statistic. 


```



```{r, fig.cap="Static Plot of Alcohol Consumption Across U.S. States", fig.width=10}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

alc_static |>
  
  ggplot(aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) + 
  
  geom_polygon(aes(fill = alcohol), color = "black") +
  
  labs(
    fill = "Alcohol Consumption in Gal/Capita", 
    x = "Longitude", 
    y = "Latitude") +
  theme_clean()

```

In this map, we can see U.S. states with different alcohol consumption rates. Most of the country falls between 2-4.5 gallons per capita. Some standout states include Utah with the lowest consumption, likely due to Mormon populations, and surprisingly New Hampshire with over 4 gallons as the highest. 
These statistics are sourced from the `states` dataset in the `poliscidata` R package, created by Philip Pollock and Barry Edwards. [https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/poliscidata/versions/2.3.0/topics/states] 



```{r, fig.cap="Interactive Plot of Alcohol Consumption Across U.S. States"}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

bins <- c(1,1.5,2,2.5,3,3.5,4,4.5)
# We choose these bins as alcohol values because they capture the minimum and maximum values, but provide enough bins that states can be distinguished.

pal <- colorBin("YlOrRd", domain = alcohol_states$alcohol, bins = bins)
# We are creating a palate based on yellow orange and red, with the set bins and alcohol statistics.


labels <- lapply(alc_int$label, HTML)
# We are converting our label column into a dynamic HTML label.


alc_int |>
leaflet() |>
  addTiles() |>
  setView(lng = -100, lat = 38, 
            zoom = 3) |>
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal(alcohol),
    #This creates the gradient across states with our custom palate
    
    weight = 2,
    opacity = 1,
    color = "black",
    dashArray = "3",
    fillOpacity = 0.7,
    highlightOptions = highlightOptions(
      weight = 5,
      color = "#666",
      dashArray = "",
      fillOpacity = 0.7,
      bringToFront = TRUE),
      label = labels,
    # Each state will be labeled with our dynamic HTML labels
    
    labelOptions = labelOptions(
      style = list("font-weight" = "normal", padding = "3px 8px"),
      textsize = "15px",
      direction = "auto")) |>
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~alcohol, opacity = 0.7, title = "Alcohol Consumption in Gal/Capita",
    position = "bottomright")
# Our legend reflects the same palate and alcohol values


```
These statistics are sourced from the `states` dataset in the `poliscidata` R package, created by Philip Pollock and Barry Edwards. [https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/poliscidata/versions/2.3.0/topics/states]


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

gay_support_states <- 
  (as_tibble(poliscidata::states)) |>
  select(state, gay_support3) |>
  mutate(
    state = str_to_lower(
      str_squish(state))
    ) |>
  mutate(
    gay_support3 = str_replace_all(
      gay_support3, 
      "Med", 
      "medium")
    ) |>
  mutate(
    gay_support3 = str_to_lower(
      gay_support3)
    ) |>
  mutate(
    gay_support3 = fct_relevel(
      gay_support3, 
      c("low", "medium", "high"))
    ) 

# We are now peeling only the categorical variable relating to gay rights support from the polysci dataset. The state names are once again made lowercase and without spaces, to join with the static and interactive state information. The category 'med' is replaced with 'medium' so that the sentence structure of the labels makes sense. Lastly, the levels are reordered from low to high so that the legend is sequential, and converted to factors so that we can create a palate in our interactive plot.
```


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

gs_static <- 
  left_join(
    states_polygon, 
    gay_support_states, 
    by = "state")

gs_int <- 
  left_join(
    states_sf, 
    gay_support_states, 
    by = "state"
    ) |>
  mutate(
    label = str_c(
      "The public support for gay rights in ", 
      state, 
      " is ", 
      gay_support3)
    ) |>
  filter(!is.na(gay_support3))


# Our gay rights support dataset is joined with the static and interactive state information, the same as before. We are also creating a label column in our interactive dataset that describes the public support level.
```



```{r, fig.cap="Static Plot of Gay Rights Support Across U.S. States", fig.width=10}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

gs_static |>
drop_na() |>
# We are dropping the NA values so that only the three categories show up  
ggplot(mapping = aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) + 
  
  geom_polygon(aes(fill = gay_support3), color = "black") +
  
  labs(fill = "Gay Rights Support Level", x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
  theme_clean()
```

This map describes 3 bins of gay rights support levels across U.S. states. In general, Northeast states and West Coast states like California and Washington are highly supportive, while the South generally expresses low support. The Midwest region shows medium support, such as Minnesota where the population is mixed between left-leaning cities and rural populations. One notable takeaway is the clear distinction of U.S. regions in gay rights support.
These statistics are sourced from the `states` dataset in the `poliscidata` R package, created by Philip Pollock and Barry Edwards. [https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/poliscidata/versions/2.3.0/topics/states]


```{r, fig.cap="Interactive Plot of Gay Rights Support Across U.S. States"}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

RdYlBu <- colorFactor("RdYlBu", domain = gay_support_states$gay_support3)
# We are using colorFactor this time, because our 3 levels are a factor, and do not need manual bins. We are choosing red yellow and blue this time as our color palate.


labels <- lapply(gs_int$label, HTML)
# Our label column is converted into an HTML interactive label

gs_int |>
leaflet() |>
  addTiles() |>
  setView(lng = -100, lat = 38, 
            zoom = 3) |>
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~RdYlBu(gay_support3),
    # Our saved color palate is used
    
    weight = 2,
    opacity = 1,
    color = "black",
    dashArray = "3",
    fillOpacity = 0.7,
    highlightOptions = highlightOptions(
      weight = 5,
      color = "#666",
      dashArray = "",
      fillOpacity = 0.7,
      bringToFront = TRUE),
      label = labels,
    labelOptions = labelOptions(
      style = list("font-weight" = "normal", padding = "3px 8px"),
      textsize = "15px",
      direction = "auto")) |>
  addLegend(pal = RdYlBu, values =  ~gay_support3, opacity = 0.7, title = "Public Support for Gay Rights",
      #Our legend uses our palate and gay support levels, as well as a description       
            
    position = "bottomright")

```

These statistics are sourced from the `states` dataset in the `poliscidata` R package, created by Philip Pollock and Barry Edwards. [https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/poliscidata/versions/2.3.0/topics/states]
